segments.text: Stereochemistry studies molecules that share the same connectivity (which atoms are bonded to which) but differ in their three-dimensional spatial arrangement — a distinction invisible in an ordinary structural formula but often critical to a molecule’s chemical and biological behaviour (most dramatically, in drugs where one stereoisomer is therapeutic and its mirror image is inactive or harmful).

items.text: Chirality (non-superimposable mirror images) most commonly arises from a stereogenic centre; a molecule with an internal symmetry plane is achiral even with apparent stereocentres present (meso compounds).

Enantiomers share all physical properties except optical rotation direction and interaction with other chiral entities; diastereomers genuinely differ in physical properties and are separable by ordinary methods.
Optical activity, measured by a polarimeter, is how enantiomers are experimentally distinguished; a racemic mixture shows zero net rotation.

CIP rules assign unambiguous R/S configuration labels based on group priority, independent of the (unrelated) direction of optical rotation; configurational isomerism (fixed) is fundamentally different from freely interconverting conformational isomerism.
